text: Everything in this chapter so far has been hand-built: info, histograms, group-bys, heatmaps. That's the right way to learn. But for a first pass on a new table, some libraries generate a whole exploration report in a few lines. This lesson looks at two: ydata-profiling and Sweetviz, and how to use them without letting them do your thinking.

ydata-profiling's ProfileReport writes a self-contained HTML file in a few seconds for a table this size: an overview, one section per variable, correlations, a missing-values view, sample rows, and a list of alerts you can also read straight from code.

On our practice data, the alerts flagged orders and total spend as highly correlated, twenty missing age values, and nineteen customers with zero orders and zero spend. That last one is a genuine question for the data owner: are those newly signed-up accounts, or ones that never purchased?

Sweetviz takes a different angle, built for comparing two datasets or a target column. sv dot compare puts a training set and a test set side by side, with target_feat showing how every variable relates to churned.

Here's what automation missed. The maximum total spend value is visible right in the statistics, but nothing in the alert list told me to be worried about it. Deciding that twenty-four fifty per order is implausible needed the spend-per-order reasoning from the last lesson, context the tool simply doesn't have.

Use these tools for a first pass, then follow up by hand on whatever looks interesting. Read every section; a report is easy to generate and easy to ignore. And never paste a report to stakeholders as the analysis. It's a set of observations, not a story.

Automated profiling catches missing values, duplicates, zeros, and strong correlations fast, but it misses context-dependent problems, so hand-built EDA still matters. That completes chapter three. Next: Power BI for data scientists, starting with connecting it to Python and SQL.
